records.title: Sand-Dredging Boats Active One Day After Ban Announced
records.originalTitle: Sand-Dredging Boats Active One Day After Ban Announced
records.publisher: Open Development Cambodia (ODC), republishing the Cambodia Daily
records.location: Meanchey district, Niroth commune, Phnom Penh, Cambodia
records.summary: Sand-dredging boats were reportedly still working on the Mekong River in Phnom Penh's Meanchey district on Tuesday. This was one day after Governor Pa Socheatvong ordered a temporary suspension of all dredging in the city. City Hall said the ban responded to an overabundance of unlicensed firms dredging river sand in the capital. A boat worker, Touch Sovann, 30, said he was dredging as usual for a firm called Sok Hong. Excavators and trucks reportedly awaited sand pumped 500 meters through pipes from the Mekong for a firm workers identified as Sok Ly. City Hall's Mr. Long Dimanche said he was unaware of continued dredging but that serious action would be taken against firms dredging during the ban.

records.title: Photographing the Disastrous Effects of Sand Mining on the Mekong River
records.originalTitle: Photographing the Disastrous Effects of Sand Mining on the Mekong River
records.location: Mekong River in Luang Prabang, Vientiane, Don Daeng Island (Champasak) and Don Khong Island in Laos; Phnom Penh, Cambodia; Mekong Delta, Viet Nam
records.summary: A first-person photo essay by a Beijing-based photographer who travelled down the Mekong in July 2016 to see the effects of sand mining. The author says sand miners have dredged the river and dug up its banks from Myanmar to Vietnam to meet regional demand for sand used in concrete and asphalt. The author reports that riverbank erosion makes the river shallower, and that locals say fishing is declining because of sand mining and dams. In Vientiane the author describes workers, some as young as 11, extracting sand from a pit for about $10 USD a day. The author also links Phnom Penh's construction growth to demand for sand. The author claims Singapore has expanded its land area by some 22 percent since the 1960s and says much of its imported sand comes from the Mekong's banks. These are the author's observations and claims and are not backed by cited data. The essay also covers dams, drought and unrelated topics such as unexploded bombs and casinos.
records.limitations: Personal narrative and anecdotal. Claims, such as those about Singapore's sand sourcing and causes of fish decline, are unsourced. The text has errors and inconsistencies, for example Lake Jiolong and the claim of more than two tons of bombs. Authorship is not given in the supplied text. Many details are not specific to sand mining. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

discovery.reason: The Mekong Delta scope and sand-extraction link are supported by the passage "40% diện tích Đồng bằng sông Cửu Long sẽ biến mất vào năm 2100 bởi thiếu hụt trầm tích mà một trong những nguyên nhân chính là việc khai khai thác cát quá mức." The draft still fails on faithfulness and evidence. The supplied article text has no headline, so the draft's title and originalTitle ("Quản lý khai thác cát bền vững để “cứu” Đồng bằng sông Cửu Long - Open Development Vietnam") cannot be verified against the source and look inferred. The draft also names Open Development Vietnam as publisher, which the supplied text does not show. Its summary adds the claim that "The article also cites excessive groundwater extraction, upstream hydropower dams and increasing river sand extraction as causes of erosion", which is stated in the text, but its figure quotes omit the date-linked statement and do not cover every number in the summary (19/12 is covered, 2100 and 40% are covered). The publisher metadata date 2022-12-23 is acceptable, but the event date 19/12 has no stated year in the body. The text is also a truncated excerpt ending in "Đọc tiếp…", yet the draft marks readType as "full body". No gold-mining content. No same-event duplicate is evident among the archive records. Rejected because of the unverifiable headline and publisher and the readType error.

The article is substantively about sand dredging on the Mekong at Ang Loeung, Peam Ro district, Prey Veng, Cambodia. It covers villagers' protest against dredging barges, a Mining Ministry official's statement on the licence, and an NGO director's comment on bank collapse. The scope passage is an exact quote and links excessive riverbed sand dredging to bank collapse, attributed to the NGO director. The English title is a faithful translation of the Khmer headline. The date comes from the publisher datePublished metadata (2026-07-07T14:10:52+00:00). The figures (more than 5 years of dredging presence, licence for more than 5 years, more than 3 km of bank collapse) are in the text. The article is not about gold mining. No nearby archive record covers this same incident, so there is no duplicate. Caveats for the summary: allegations come from anonymous residents and political figures, the company did not comment, and the article does not establish causation for the specific collapse.

Other minor problems in the draft: it names the publisher as 'Mekong Youth (WordPress)', which the article text does not support, and it lists the Tatai River under specificRivers, though that is only background.

reviews.reviewReason: The article is a first-person photo essay substantively about sand mining along the Mekong. The scope quote ("For decades, sand miners have dredged the river and dug up its banks along stretches from Myanmar to Vietnam to feed an unsuitable regional demand for tiny grains of sand") directly links the piece to sand extraction in the basin. It names specific Mekong places in Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, and the date 2017-11-27T11:15:00+00:00 comes from publisher metadata. The headline translation is faithful because the title is already in English. The piece is not about gold mining. No archive record is the same event. Caveats: the claims are anecdotal and unsourced, including the Singapore sourcing claim, the 22 percent land-gain figure and the fish decline attribution. The text also contains errors, and the draft's country list should be limited to countries actually supported (Myanmar and China are only mentioned in passing).
